title: quick-synth-experiment-rundown-miguel
content:
Purpose: quick, one-page tracker for small synthetic-input sweeps. Keep results readable at-a-glance, capture surprises, next actions. For my own use while iterating on quant cfgs and batch/window policies.

Context / setup:
- workload: short-chat-turns (avg. 30 tokens request, 60 tokens response) synthetic prompt set (50 prompts, mixed domain).
- infra: local dedicated small GPU node (A100-split), runtime build from branch perf/fast-kernels-1423.
- models: gptx-13b baseline FP16, gptx-13b-4bit, gptx-7b-q8
- measurement: p50/p95 latency measured at client (end-to-end), token cost rough calc using internal unit pricing for hosted-equivalent.
- each row = single config run (3k requests simulated, concurrent clients 8 unless noted).

Quick table (space-delimited columns — copyable):
RUN_ID  MODEL           QUANT   BATCH  P50_MS  P95_MS  TOKENS/REQ  COST/1kTOKENS  QUALITY(0-1)  NOTES
r001    gptx-13b        fp16    1      84      165     90          $2.40           0.88          baseline, warm cache
r002    gptx-13b        fp16    8      110     260     90          $0.30           0.88          batching increases latency tail
r003    gptx-13b        4bit    1      97      190     90          $0.96           0.86          slight quality drop, memory good
r004    gptx-13b        4bit    16     170     420     90          $0.06           0.86          throughput up, severe p95
r005    gptx-7b-q8       q8      1      55      120     90          $0.72           0.80          cheap+fast, lower quality
r006    gptx-7b-q8       q8      32     210     600     90          $0.02           0.80          big batching hurt tail, but cost tiny
r007    gptx-13b        4bit    4      125     310     90          $0.24           0.86          moderate batching, p95 still high

Observations / quick takeaways:
- For small chat turns, single-request FP16 p50 is acceptable (84ms) but cost high. 4-bit holds quality fairly well (~2% drop) and halves memory/cost.
- Aggressive batching (>=16) increases p95 severely on this local rig — likely queuing/KV cache contention. Not suitable for latency-sensitive endpoints.
- 7b q8 is attractive for non-core flows (search summaries, quick assistant hints). Good p50 and lowest cost per token.
- p95 behavior correlates with batch size and concurrent clients; need to test with different concurrency shapes.

Open questions / notes to self:
- Is the p95 degradation GPU-bound (kernel scheduling) or host-side (request queue)? Add nvprof / traces next run.
- Try adaptive-batching: small-window for <50-token responses, larger batches for >200 token jobs.
- Compare 4-bit quantization using per-channel vs uniform quant: cost/latency delta?
- Validate with real user prompts (not just synthetic) before recommending to product for Dedicated pool.

Planned next runs (short checklist):
- [ ] run nvprof on r004 to capture kernel timelines (ticket: JIRA-INF-681)
- [ ] simulate mixed traffic (20% long chats) to see cache pressure
- [ ] repeat r003 with different compile flags (use fused-kv1)
- [ ] run 7b-q8 @ lower concurrency (clients=2) to measure p95 baseline

Summary decision (draft):
- For latency-critical endpoints keep batch <=4 and prefer 4-bit on 13b only if quality is verified on real prompts.
- Use 7b-q8 for low-cost non-SLO endpoints.

Random notes / scratch lines:
- saved copy: perf/notes/quick-synth-2025-11-02.md
- reminded to ping @noah about sample seed variance (Slack: #perf-experiments)
- quick cost calc: cost/1k = (tokens_per_req * reqs_per_1k / 1000) * unit_token_price -> sanity check numbers above

If I revisit this doc: add short graph (p50 vs batch, p95 vs conc) and paste nvprof snippets.

-- Miguel
